title: Can you build your own AI order processing as a small retail supplier?
summary: AI order processing can take manual order entry off your desk, but can you build it yourself? See what small suppliers in Europe are building, what can go wrong, and when to connect instead.
body_markdown:
AI order processing lets a small business read an incoming order from an email, a PDF or a spreadsheet and enter it in its ERP with little or no typing. It is easier to get than ever, and some companies now build it themselves.


But AI that speeds up automated order entry does not connect you to your retailers, keep up with their changing rules or answer for mistakes.


The build-your-own trend is real. In McKinsey's 2026 State of AI survey,[32 percent of respondents](https://www.mckinsey.com/capabilities/quantumblack/our-insights/the-state-of-ai) said their organization had decided against buying at least one software product or feature because it could be built in-house with AI coding tools. However, just because more organizations show less eagerness to buy new solutions thanks to AI does not mean the replacement works 100% of the time.


This article looks at what small businesses in Europe are actually building, what can go wrong, and where one shared connection to your retailers, suppliers and logistics providers does the job better.


## **Why are small businesses using AI to replace manual order entry?**


Because manual order entry is slow, and the tools to automate it are now within reach of teams without developers. "Vibe coding" means describing what you want in plain language and letting an AI write the software.


Here are examples of what that already looks like in practice:


-


**The Netherlands.** The manufacturing trade body FME[runs a vibe coding programme](https://www.fme.nl/agenda/vibe-coding-de-maakindustrie-van-idee-naar-werkende-applicatie) for professionals who can't program, so they leave with a working prototype for their own organization. A[Dutch business article](https://www.dezaak.nl/blog-content/apps-bouwen-zonder-te-programmeren-hoe-ai-het-speelveld-verandert-voor-ondernemers/) tells of the director of a 20-person company who built his own HR system and cancelled the package he was paying for.


-


**Germany.** An 18-person timber construction business received inquiries by email, WhatsApp and phone, and its office spent about 1.5 hours a day sorting them. According to the consultancy[SIMO](https://simo-online.com/en/blog/vibe-coding-fuer-kmu-so-baust-du-interne-tools-ohne-dev) , the company built an intake form and an automation that uses AI to categorize each inquiry and write it to the CRM, saving about 8 hours a week. The owner did not read every line of the AI-written script but checked every step. These were customer inquiries rather than retailer purchase orders, but the pattern is the same. The idea is also reaching purchase orders: Munich-based[Comena](https://www.ycombinator.com/companies/comena) builds AI agents that automate email orders to ERP entry for distributors and manufacturers, and says they plug straight in if the customer's ERP already supports EDI.


Across Europe, small teams are using AI to take routine admin off their desks, from building their own tools to reading email orders, and software firms now sell ready-made agents for the same job. Building a tool is one thing, though, and keeping it running is another, so here is what can go wrong.


## **Build vs buy: what can go wrong with a do-it-yourself AI build?**


The main risks of building your own AI order tool are:


-


- **Security flaws** (weaknesses that let outsiders reach your data)
